title: Cylinders or spheres pressed into full surface contact form hexagons

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cylinders or spheres pressed into full surface contact form hexagons

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Whenever cylinders or spheres of similar size are brought into complete surface contact by any uniform force (surface tension, growth pressure or external pressure), they tend to form a pattern of hexagons in section or surface view, each meeting six neighbours with 120° angles.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: uniform pressure on similar cylinders or spheres \Rightarrow hexagons, 6 neighbours, angles 120^\circ

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: wherever we have a system of cylinders or spheres, associated together with sufficient mutual interaction to bring them into complete surface contact, there, in section or in surface view, we tend to get a pattern of hexagons.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter VII, “The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates”; topic “Hexagonal patterns from close packing”. Scope: epithelia, plant parenchyma, coral corallites, insect combs and other close-packed bodies of uniform size

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: uniform pressure on similar cylinders or spheres \Rightarrow hexagons, 6 neighbours, angles 120^\circ

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch07-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The packing prediction is mathematically precise and straightforward to extract from images. Existing data test several biological subclasses, but not the universal range of materials and force types stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For packed objects of known size dispersion and contact completeness, measure neighbour number, sidedness, and junction angles and test convergence toward six neighbours and 120-degree junctions.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The claim spans non-equivalent cylinders, spheres, sections, and surfaces.

Size variation and boundary effects alter neighbour counts.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.94
discriminating power: 0.82
data adequacy: 0.55
analysis feasibility: 0.8
data existence: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The packing prediction can be scored with neighbour counts and angles on data that already exist for epithelia, comb and corals. The informative contrast is complete facial contact versus cylinders that only touch locally. That comparison is standard image analysis and is sufficient to confirm or refute the stated tendency, with the topological average kept in view as a bias.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Wherever similar cylinders or spheres are in complete surface contact, measure neighbour number and junction angle in section or surface view, and compare them with loose bundles that do not touch along faces. Complete contact yielding hexagons with angles near 120 degrees, and incomplete contact leaving round profiles, would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Any trivalent tiling averages six sides, so neighbour number alone is a weak discriminator and angle plus completeness of contact have to carry the test.

Scans and segmentations over-represent model plants, honeybees and a few coral colonies.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.6
operationalizability: 0.9
data existence: 0.75
discriminating power: 0.65
